title: Apparitions and private revelation (CCC 67)
hook: no apparition is required belief, even approved ones

segments.voice: Yesterday, Częstochowa: a Black Madonna with sword cuts on her cheek, and a legend about Saint Luke that Catholics may hold lightly. Your line was the scarred icon.

A woman at a parish fish fry says, between bites, that she's never been sure about Lourdes. The man across from her nearly drops his fork. Doesn't the Church approve it? Isn't that part of being Catholic? The next days make it urgent: a grotto in France, a field in Portugal, a church wall in Ireland, a school in Rwanda, a forest in Vietnam, all places where people say Mary appeared. First, the rule the Church uses for all of them. It's short, it's in the Catechism, and it may surprise the man with the fork.
screen: `NEVER SURE ABOUT LOURDES.` → `PLACES WHERE PEOPLE SAY MARY APPEARED.` → `FIRST, THE RULE.`

segments.voice: Begin with public revelation. The Letter to the Hebrews says God spoke in many ways through the prophets, and then, in the Douay-Rheims, "last of all, in these days hath spoken to us by his Son." The Catechism draws the conclusion: in Christ, God has said everything, and no new public revelation is to be expected before Christ comes again. That's the faith the whole Church holds and hands on. Then paragraph sixty-seven, and the other kind. Over the centuries, it says, there have been so-called private revelations, some recognized by the Church's authority. Private doesn't mean secret; a crowd might see it. It means they don't belong to the deposit of faith. Their job isn't to improve or complete Christ's revelation, but to help people live by it more fully in a particular time. Next, what approval means. When the Church approves a reported apparition, it's saying, in effect: nothing here contradicts the faith, and you may honor it. It isn't saying every Catholic is bound to believe it happened. The woman at the fish fry is free to stay unsure. The man is free to make a pilgrimage. Neither is a better Catholic for it. Last, the attitude. Paul gives one to an early church: "Despise not prophecies. But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Not scorn, and not swallowing everything: testing, and keeping what's good.
screen: `IN CHRIST, GOD HAS SAID EVERYTHING.` · `PRIVATE: OUTSIDE THE DEPOSIT OF FAITH.` · `APPROVED MEANS PERMITTED, NOT REQUIRED.` · `TEST IT, KEEP WHAT'S GOOD.` · then, large: `PROVE ALL THINGS; HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a story you've heard of a vision, a healing or a sign, and notice which way you lean: toward it, wanting it true, or away, ready to roll your eyes. Neither lean is wrong; just notice it, and hold the story the way you'd hold something fragile that belongs to someone else, open hand, no squeezing. If you pray, ask for the grace to keep what's good.
Private revelation. A vision or message, even a public one, that isn't part of the faith the whole Church must believe. It can help people live the Gospel; it can never add to it. Today's word.
Your line: never required. Approved means permitted, not required. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church distinguishes public revelation, completed in Christ, from private revelations such as approved apparitions; Catholics may honor approved apparitions and visit their shrines, but are not required to believe in them.

chat.says: If the Church approves an apparition like Lourdes, do Catholics have to believe it?
options: No. Approval means nothing in it contradicts the faith and it may be honored, but no one is bound.
Yes. Once approved, it becomes part of the deposit of faith that every Catholic must hold.
Only if a crowd saw it; a vision seen by a crowd is public revelation and binds everyone.
chat.meaning: Private revelations don't belong to the deposit of faith. Approval permits honoring one; it doesn't require anyone to believe it.

CCC 65–67 paraphrased (God has said everything in the Word; no new public revelation before Christ's glorious manifestation; private revelations, some recognized, do not belong to the deposit of faith; their role is to help live more fully by Christ's revelation in a certain period). The Catechism's wording is copyrighted, so nothing is quoted.

The description of what approval means ('nothing contradicts the faith, and you may honor it', not 'you must believe') is a general summary; the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith's 2024 norms use new terms (e.g. nihil obstat). Confirm the summary is fair.
The hook lists places the coming days visit (France, Portugal, Ireland, Rwanda, Vietnam); Guadalupe and Vailankanni also follow. Confirm the framing.
